d.title: Four serving shapes, measured, with the capacity each implies
d.caption: The latencies are measured and the capacities follow from them: one synchronous worker handles about **82 req/s** at p99 through the scikit-learn pipeline, **1,961** through ONNX, and **35** through FastAPI's validation layer. So 500 req/s needs 7, 1 and 15 workers respectively. Note the inversion in the batch column — ONNX is forty times faster per request and *slower* in batch here, because its one-hot of string categoricals does not vectorise.

d.title: Training–serving skew is a consequence of having two implementations
d.caption: It is not a risk to be managed with care; it is arithmetic. If features are computed by training code and again by serving code, the two will diverge — on a rounding rule, a default, a category spelling, a time zone. Serialising the **fitted pipeline** and calling that object in both places removes the second implementation, and with it the possibility.

nodes.label: They diverge
nodes.sub: a default, a rounding rule, a time zone

nodes.label: A golden set on reload
nodes.sub: catches it if it ever returns

d.title: Data drift and concept drift need different monitors
d.caption: Data drift is P(X) moving: the inputs changed. Concept drift is P(Y|X) moving: the **relationship** changed. A model can be perfectly right under data drift and perfectly wrong under concept drift with inputs that look identical — which is why the second monitor needs labels, and therefore always arrives late.
cells: can it tell old from new rows

d.title: ADWIN: let the window decide its own length
d.caption: A fixed window has to be chosen in advance, and the right length depends on a drift you have not seen yet. ADWIN keeps a growing window and repeatedly asks whether some split of it has two halves whose means differ by more than chance — if so, the old part is dropped. The window shortens itself exactly when the world changes and grows again when it is stable, which is the behaviour a fixed window can only approximate.

d.title: Shadow, canary, A/B — three different questions
d.caption: They are not stages of one process, they answer different things. **Shadow** asks 'does it run and agree' with no user exposed. **Canary** asks 'does it break anything' on a small share. **A/B** is the only one that asks 'is it better', because that needs randomisation and a business metric. Skipping to A/B means debugging a service in front of real users.

nodes.label: Is it better?
nodes.sub: the business metric; only this answers it

d.title: What has to exist before a model is allowed to serve
d.caption: The rollback entry is the one that gets deferred and the one that is needed at 3 a.m. A registry that can name the previous version, and a deployment that can return to it in one step, is what turns a bad release into an incident of minutes rather than hours.

d.title: Three answers to 'what is the parameter', on three heads out of three
d.caption: The MLE says the coin always lands heads, which is the honest maximum of the likelihood and a useless forecast. MAP adds a prior and returns a single number; the posterior returns the **distribution**, and everything else in this lesson is a consequence of carrying it instead of collapsing it.
cells: p = 1.0: it will never land tails

d.title: The predictive variance grows with distance from the data
d.caption: Five points, σ² = 1, τ² = 4. Two things to read. First, the posterior mean [1.9619, 1.5317] **is** the ridge estimate with λ = σ²/τ² = 0.25, exactly — MAP is penalised fitting, as 1.4 claimed. Second, the two sources of uncertainty add in quadrature: the noise contributes 1.000 at every x, while the **parameter** contribution grows from 0.436 at x = 0 to 3.154 at x = 10, so the total sd goes 1.091 to 3.309. A point estimate cannot express that, and it is the whole reason to carry the posterior.

d.title: A Gaussian process is a prior over functions
d.caption: Instead of putting a prior on a weight vector, put one directly on the function: any finite set of inputs has a joint Gaussian over their outputs, with the covariance given by a kernel. Conditioning on the observed points gives a posterior that passes near the data and **fans out between and beyond** it. The kernel is the modelling choice — it encodes smoothness, periodicity, length scale — and the cost is the O(n³) inversion that keeps GPs to thousands of points.

nodes.label: A prior over functions
nodes.sub: any finite set is jointly Gaussian

nodes.label: Variance fans out between them
nodes.sub: uncertainty where there is no data

d.title: When there is no closed form: three ways to approximate a posterior
d.caption: They trade accuracy against cost in opposite directions. MCMC is asymptotically exact and slow, and its diagnostics tell you when to distrust it. Variational inference is fast and systematically **under-estimates** the variance, because minimising the reverse KL prefers a narrow mode. Laplace is a single Gaussian at the mode and is cheapest of all.
cells: cheapest; wrong for skew or multimodality

d.title: The acquisition function is where exploration is decided
d.caption: A surrogate model gives a mean and a variance at every untried point; the acquisition function turns those two numbers into one score to maximise. **Expected improvement** weighs how much better a point might be by how likely that is, so it naturally samples both near the best-so-far and where the model is simply ignorant — which is why it needs no explicit exploration parameter.

nodes.label: Surrogate over the space
nodes.sub: a GP: mean and variance everywhere

nodes.label: Update and repeat
nodes.sub: the surrogate sharpens where it looked

d.title: Why the posterior makes a good policy
d.caption: Thompson sampling needs no exploration parameter at all: drawing one sample per arm from each posterior and playing the best explores exactly in proportion to how uncertain the arm is, and that proportion shrinks on its own as evidence arrives.

cells.text: acting randomly epsilon of the time

d.title: Prequential evaluation: test on each row before training on it
d.caption: There is no held-out set on a stream, so the honest protocol is to predict each arriving row, record the error, and *then* learn from it. Every row is therefore a test row exactly once, and the running error is an unbiased picture of how the model behaved as the data arrived.

d.title: Detecting drift on a stream, and what each detector watches
d.caption: A drift detector watches a **statistic**, and which statistic decides what it can see. Error-rate detectors need labels and so fire late; input-distribution detectors fire early and cannot tell a harmless population shift from a damaging one. Running both and comparing is what distinguishes 'more of some customers' from 'the relationship changed'.

d.title: Federated averaging, one round
d.caption: The data never moves; the **model** does. Each client trains locally for a few steps and returns its update, the server averages them weighted by how many rows each client held, and the new global model goes back out. One round is a weighted average of gradients that were each computed on a different distribution — which is exactly why non-IID clients make this converge slowly, or to the wrong place.

nodes.label: Each trains locally
nodes.sub: a few steps, on its own rows

d.title: Non-IID is not one problem
d.caption: Federated averaging degrades for different reasons depending on **how** the clients differ, and the fix differs with it. Label skew is the one that breaks naive averaging hardest: each client's update points at its own label distribution, and the average of those directions need not help anyone.
cells: personalisation: one model cannot fit all

d.title: What an update leaks, and what it costs to hide it
d.caption: Keeping the data local is not privacy. A gradient is a function of the rows that produced it, and from it an attacker can often recover whether a particular record was present — sometimes the record itself. Differential privacy bounds that by **clipping and adding noise**, and the bound is paid for in accuracy: a smaller ε is a stronger guarantee and a worse model.

nodes.label: Membership inference
nodes.sub: was this record in the batch?

d.title: Collaborative filtering by hand, and why five users is not enough
d.caption: With two or three co-rated items per pair, the correlations come out at **±1.000** — Ann–Di is −1.000 on two co-ratings, which carries no information at all. The user-based estimate for Ann on i3 is 3.000, driven entirely by that spurious −1. The item-based route is worse: its similarities are also ±1 and the prediction lands at **−2.717**, off the rating scale entirely. The arithmetic is correct and the data cannot support it.

d.title: Matrix factorisation: learn the factors, never form the matrix
d.caption: A users × items matrix of a million by a hundred thousand has 10¹¹ cells and perhaps 10⁷ observed ratings. Factorisation never builds it: it learns a short vector per user and per item such that their dot product reproduces the **observed** entries, and the unobserved ones fall out as predictions. ALS alternates two least-squares solves; SGD walks the observed entries one at a time.

nodes.label: Observed ratings only
nodes.sub: a sparse list, not a matrix

d.title: Implicit feedback: a click is not a rating, and a non-click is not a 'no'
d.caption: With explicit ratings the unobserved entries are genuinely unknown and are skipped. With clicks there are **no negatives at all** — an item not clicked may never have been shown. That changes the objective: WRMF treats every unobserved pair as a weak negative with a confidence weight, and BPR gives up on absolute scores and optimises the **ranking** of a clicked item above a sampled unclicked one.

d.title: The cold start is a certainty, so the fallback is part of the design
d.caption: Collaborative filtering of every kind needs interactions, and a new user or item has none. Every production recommender therefore has a **cascade**, and the honest version decides in advance what each stage falls back to — because the alternative is a new item that is structurally invisible until somebody happens to find it.

d.title: The feedback loop, and why offline ranking metrics flatter the old system
d.caption: Held-out clicks were generated by **what the old system chose to show**. A model that reproduces those choices scores well; a model that would have surfaced something better scores badly, because the user never had the chance to click it. Popularity bias compounds it, which is why popularity is a strong offline baseline and a weak product.

d.title: Tokens, stems and lemmas
d.caption: Stemming chops suffixes by rule, so it is fast and produces non-words; lemmatisation looks the word up and needs its part of speech to be right. For a linear model on TF-IDF the difference is usually worth less than the time it costs — which is the finding worth having before reaching for a transformer.

d.title: TF-IDF, worked: why the weight is a product of two opposite things
d.caption: Term frequency rewards a word for appearing often **in this document**; inverse document frequency punishes it for appearing in **many** documents. Their product is high only for a word that is frequent here and rare elsewhere — which is the definition of distinctive. The L2 normalisation at the end is what makes a long document and a short one comparable.

d.title: Eight text pipelines on four newsgroups, measured
d.caption: Read the first three rows: switching from counts to TF-IDF buys **2.9 points**, and switching from multinomial to ComplementNB buys another 2.2 — and the whole thing fits and predicts in half a second. The tuned logistic regression and LinearSVC do not beat it. This is the measurement to have in hand before anyone proposes fine-tuning a transformer on four thousand documents.

d.title: Cosine on TF-IDF, and what BM25 adds
d.caption: Both rank documents by weighted term overlap. BM25 adds two things TF-IDF lacks: a **saturating** term frequency, so the tenth occurrence of a word adds almost nothing, and an explicit length normalisation with a tunable strength rather than the implicit one that L2 gives.

d.title: LDA: a document is a mixture of topics, a topic a distribution over words
d.caption: The generative story is the model: pick a topic mixture for the document, then for each word pick a topic from that mixture and a word from that topic. Fitting inverts the story. Two consequences people trip over: the number of topics is an input that the data does not choose for you, and the topics are **unlabelled** — the names are yours, read off the top words, and nothing guarantees they are coherent.

d.title: The perceptron cannot do XOR, and one hidden layer can
d.caption: XOR is not linearly separable, so no single linear boundary classifies it — that is the result that stalled the field for a decade. A hidden layer fixes it by **re-representing** the input: two units carve the plane into regions where the classes *are* separable, and the output layer draws one line in that new space. Everything about depth is this idea repeated.

nodes.label: Two hidden units
nodes.sub: each a line, with a non-linearity

d.title: Backpropagation on two weights, every number
d.caption: The network is x → σ(w₁x) → σ(w₂h) with x = 1, y = 1, w₁ = 0.5, w₂ = −0.4. Read the backward block: each line is one factor of the chain rule, and the **same** ∂L/∂ŷ × ∂ŷ/∂z₂ is reused for both weights — that reuse is the entire efficiency of backpropagation. Note ∂L/∂w₁ = +0.0130 is positive while ∂L/∂w₂ = −0.0861 is negative, because w₂ is negative and flips the sign on the way back.

state: x w2 x h(1-h) x x

d.title: Activation, learning rate and batch size, and what each one breaks
d.caption: Three dials with three distinct failure modes. A saturating activation kills the gradient at both ends; a learning rate above the stability limit diverges exactly as in 1.8; and a batch size changes the gradient's **noise**, which is a regulariser — so raising it without lowering the learning rate often loses accuracy rather than gaining it.
cells: it is the saturation either way

d.title: Four regularisers, and the one that is not what it looks like
d.caption: Weight decay is L2 by another name, and early stopping is the same regulariser applied through time rather than through the objective. Dropout is the one worth understanding properly: at training time it removes units at random, which makes the network an **ensemble of subnetworks** — and at test time it is off, with the weights scaled, which is why forgetting `model.eval()` quietly degrades every prediction.

d.title: When a network beats gradient boosting on a table
d.caption: Rarely, and for specific reasons. On a small heterogeneous table boosting wins and a regularised linear model is the yardstick — as this course's churn data showed. A network earns its place when there is a representation to **learn** or to share, which a boosted tree cannot do at all.
cells: a network's weights are not readable

d.title: The fairness criteria are mutually incompatible, provably
d.caption: When the base rates differ between groups, equal TPR and equal PPV cannot both hold — that is an impossibility theorem, not a tuning problem. So a team must state which criterion it is claiming and accept the consequence named in the last column. Dropping the protected attribute does not help: it is reconstructable from the other columns.

d.title: A confounder and a collider need opposite treatment
d.caption: This is the asymmetry that makes 'control for everything' wrong. Adjusting for a confounder removes bias; adjusting for a collider **creates** it. No amount of data distinguishes them — only a causal diagram does, which is why the diagram comes before the regression.

cells.text: on the path X to Y

cells: use it, do not adjust for it

d.title: Uplift: four kinds of customer, and only one is worth treating
d.caption: A churn model ranks by **risk**; an uplift model ranks by how much the treatment *changes* the outcome, and those are different orderings. The sure things would have stayed anyway, so the discount is wasted; the lost causes leave regardless; and the sleeping dogs are actively harmed by being contacted. Only the persuadables repay the intervention — and identifying them needs a randomised experiment, because it is a question about a counterfactual.

d.title: The system-design round, and the order that answers it
d.caption: The model is one box out of eight, and candidates who start there lose the round. The feature store is where most follow-up questions land, because it is the component that has to serve the **same** definition online and offline — and the point-in-time join is the thing that makes that hard.

d.title: From scratch, and the checks that prove it
d.caption: Writing an algorithm from scratch is only half the question — the other half is how you know it is right. Each of these checks is cheap and each catches a different class of bug: a closed form agrees to machine precision, a library agrees to tolerance, a finite-difference gradient catches a sign error, and a degenerate input catches the division by zero that real data will find.
